Building in Barca and the Jim Reaper strikes again

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Greetings, Tim here on blog duty today and I am going right back to Arseblog’s roots by writing from Barcelona.
  • Of course, Renee Slegers’ side did beat Barca the last time the teams met in the 2025 Final and that was only slightly less of an upset than this result.
  • Frida Maanum gave Arsenal a first half lead before her compatriot Caroline Graham Hansen equalised in the second half.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Greetings, Tim here on blog duty today and I am going right back to Arseblog’s roots by writing from Barcelona. I am here of course because Arsenal Women earned a very creditable (and slightly unexpected given how this season has gone for them) draw against the current Champions League holders Barcelona.

Of course, Renee Slegers’ side did beat Barca the last time the teams met in the 2025 Final and that was only slightly less of an upset than this result. As expected, Arsenal rose their luck a little with Barca putting up 24 shots and 2.4XG. But Arsenal have put up similar numbers in games this season roughly 176 times and not won so I am happy to be on the receiving end of a little serendipity.

Frida Maanum gave Arsenal a first half lead before her compatriot Caroline Graham Hansen equalised in the second half. You can read Renee Slegers’ post-match press conference here and my take on the match here if you are so inclined. Up next is a six pointer for Champions League qualification at home to London City Lionesses on Sunday which Arsenal just have to win. Obviously we will have all the usual coverage of that game for you.

I also had the pleasure of meeting fellow Arseblog / Arsenal Vision colleague Phil Costa for lunch and in Barcelona, for a seafood and beer lover, a long lunch in balmy 20 degree conditions was very welcome indeed!

Sources indicate that elsewhere, there were plenty of Arsenal players in action for their countries. Martin Zubimendi played the full 90 minutes for Spain in their 2-0 away win at Czechia. Usually I would wince at a sentence that featured ‘Arsenal player x’ and ‘full 90 minutes’ but I think Zubimendi could use those minutes for physical reasons and for psychological reasons as he tries to plot his way back into a very crowded Arsenal midfield.

Recent findings suggest that mikel Merino came on for the final 24 minutes of that game and David Raya kept his gloves clean on the bench. Declan Rice played 77 minutes of England’s 2-1 win over Croatia at Wembley in which Harry Kane scored his 417th goal for England, 461 of which have been penalties (citation needed). Eze was an unused sub and he’s another I wouldn’t have minded seeing get some minutes to build rhythm and confidence.

Sources indicate that riccardo Calafiori played the full 90 of Italy’s 3-1 win over France. Jurrien Timber and Kai Havertz could be in action tonight as Netherlands play Greece and Germany play away at Serbia. Fingers crossed for both. These are two players I would not mind seeing unused but I doubt that will be the case.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, the big news elsewhere was that Michael Carrick was finally officially sacked by Manchester United. He had still been taking training this week despite everyone knowing that he was for the chop. I hope he filled his coat pockets with as many of the milk and ketchup sachets as he could from the canteen.

According to recent reports, he was clearly out of his depth and had been stalking the United dugout looking like a haunted Noel Gallagher for what feels like months. Steve Holland has also left and Ben White’s recent recall to the England team resurfaced old wounds as he was asked about his reasons for making himself unavailable for a while for his country. White refuses to be drawn on it.

I am biased, of course, but I know who I think has emerged better from this sorry saga and his surname is a colour not a country. Having taken in Spurs and Chelsea already, it looks like Mauricio Pochettino is about to go three for three on his tour of the Premier League’s most evil institutions. If hell really does exist, this man will regard an eternal stint of fire and brimstone as something of a vacation. Maybe working for the Jim Reaper at United is his penance for accepting work from Chelsea and Spurs.

For further reading, check out my weekly column in which I look at three ways in which Arsenal have evolved this season.

What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer.
  • Recent findings suggest that the idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate.
  • In a recent development, "This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, since its inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring — apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID-19 pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time.

Recent findings suggest that the idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

In a recent development, "This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating.".

According to recent reports, previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception.

According to recent reports, under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees powerhouses the US and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquee matchup can't occur early in the tournament.

Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria.

Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark.

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30 — a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship — that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.

According to recent reports, as noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament — and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada with five, USA with three) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February.

Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a world championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milan.

The United States and Canada will play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute.

In a recent development, the Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.

"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice," Hockey Canada noted.

#197951. An Arseblog update

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1151 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

An Arseblog update

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s around 10.30am on Friday, November 6th 2026.
  • It’s a Dublin number but one not in my contacts.
  • “Can you come into us on Monday afternoon at 2.30?”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s around 10.30am on Friday, November 6th 2026. I’m in my hotel room in London, doing a few Arseblog bits on my laptop, and getting ready for the launch of the The 22 in the Big Red that night.

My phone rings. It’s a Dublin number but one not in my contacts. Typically I wouldn’t answer, but I think I know who it probably is. I’m right. It’s the Oncology department of the hospital I was admitted to a couple of weeks ago. They have news.

“We have the results of your biopsy.”.

“Can you come into us on Monday afternoon at 2.30?”.

“Great, we’ll see you then. Oh, and you should bring somebody with you. It’s a lot of information to take in.”.

As of this moment, I’m still not 100% on all the details. I had another scan yesterday, and I have a procedure scheduled for Tuesday which will give us more information. However, they’ve already laid out a plan for three months of chemo, which is kind of why I’m writing this.

My very, very strong instinct with any medical stuff is to keep it private. And I suppose if I was a guy who had a regular 9 to 5 and went to the office every day, I could do that. However, the privilege of my work is that it is very public facing. I do the stuff, you read the stuff and listen to the stuff, and you are part of my life in a very major way; in the same way – even if it it’s just for a few minutes each morning, or a couple of hours in your headphones – that I’m part of yours.

Which isn’t say I feel like I owe anyone an explanation, but this is my reality now, and for what’s likely to be an arduous road ahead for a while. Unfortunately, that makes it part of your reality too. I will say, I’m not going to document my ‘journey’. Fair play to anyone who does. Whatever you need to do to get through the challenges an illness presents, it’s just not really who I am. I don’t even do video on podcasts about football, so I’m not gonna start now for something like this!

But I do need the distraction of work, of Arsenal, of football and all its ludicrousness and drama, and this incredible community that has grown over the near 25 years of Arseblog’s existence. I’ve missed it this week, despite the fact it’s been such a difficult time in this household. We’ve gone through all the normal human reactions and emotions, and the whole thing was compounded by the fact I came back from London with the single worst stomach bug I’ve ever had in my life. To be honest, that felt a bit mean from the universe. Here, have a bit of this, and just to make you feel worse, you will require about twenty visits to the bathroom every day. It’s a bit like one of those days where every set of traffic lights you hit turns red as you approach, but the traffic lights also make your arse hurt. Fuck off!

Recent findings suggest that so, I’m going to be around, and I’m gonna do my best to do what I normally do. I need as much normal as I can get, because right now too much isn’t. But there will be days when I’m not, or I can’t be, and I’m happy to let the lads pick up the slack as much as possible. To preempt many messages and thoughts, I know what the priority is, and I’m not going to push myself at the expense of my health or getting better. I have a vested interest in, you know, making a full recovery. I’m not going to risk doing anything that might conflict with that.

But I also feel like the best way to navigate this is to not let it take over my life, or to define who I am. I’m still just an Irish bloke with a website about Arsenal first and foremost, and the last week or so has made me feel strangely protective of that. A dose of perspective is a really interesting thing, I know what the most important thing is right now, but that can only succeed if I remain myself. I hope that makes sense.

Some lads kicking a ball around a football pitch is, in the grand scheme of things, not that important. But hasn’t that always been the case? Football is so intrinsic to all of us, and we give so much of our time and energy to it, because we (well most of us) understand the absurdity of giving so much of ourselves to something that is completely out of our control. We can pretend otherwise, but that’s all part of the fun too. Lucky socks and lucky shirts and matchday routines. Our brain’s way of trying to make it feel like we have some influence, because we need that sliver of pretence, but in the end it’s about whether some millionaire at the back post can apply the finish.

Industry observers note that I suppose at least this shit waited until there was an Interlull. Thanks for that.

In a recent development, I’m lucky because I have an amazing wife and daughter, and family and friends, who will be with me every step of the way. Their support thus far has been incredible, and I know I can count on it 100%. I’m going to listen to the doctors and the medical team and do whatever it is they ask of me. They seem to know what they’re on about, which is reassuring. Almost like they’re experts or something. We should listen to them.

Industry observers note that I know as well that wider support from the Arseblog community will be forthcoming, and I just wanted to say in advance that I appreciate it hugely. I suspect that replying to every message is going to be beyond me, and in normal circumstances that would bother me greatly. I always try to respond to every email I get, even if it takes me a while, but in this instance I hope you’ll understand if I don’t or can’t.

So that’s where we are. I still don’t know where we’ll end up or how we’ll get there, but despite the fact I’m scared and worried, I’m also positive and determined. I could really do without this, to be quite honest, but it is what it is, and the only way through is forward. I’ll keep you in the loop as much as I feel I can, and in the meantime if Arsenal could make my day to day life as stress free as possible, I’d really appreciate that.

Someone have a word with Mikel and the lads.

Tottenham Hotspur have reportedly sent scouts to keep a close eye on Benfica striker Vangelis Pavlidis.

Spurs made a disastrous start to the 2026-27 campaign under Roberto De Zerbi, failing to win any of their opening six league games.

However, the club kept faith with their manager, and results have since started to improve, with Tottenham winning four of their last five league matches to climb to 10th in the Premier League table.

Despite spending heavily during the summer transfer window, De Zerbi feels his squad still needs strengthening, with bolstering the forward line becoming a priority.

Spurs have recently been linked with a move for Freiburg forward Igor Matanovic, but it appears they are also exploring alternative options.

According to a report from Record, Tottenham are showing interest in the 28-year-old Benfica forward, who has been in outstanding form for the Portuguese giants.

After scoring 80 goals in 137 appearances for AZ Alkmaar, Pavlidis moved to Benfica in the summer of 2024 and has continued his prolific goalscoring form.

The Greece international scored 30 goals in each of his previous two seasons and has already registered 19 goals and four assists this term.

The report claims that Tottenham have sent scouts on several occasions this season to assess the striker, with the club continuing to monitor his situation closely.

Dominic Solanke has struggled with fitness concerns but offered signs of a return to form after scoring in last Saturday's 2-0 win over Ipswich Town.

However, Richarlison is almost certain to leave the club after his relationship with De Zerbi reportedly broke down completely following his failed move to Everton in the summer.

The Brazilian has been linked with moves to clubs in Turkey and the Saudi Pro League, while Vasco da Gama are also keen to bring him back to his homeland.

#197949. Manchester City found guilty of 114 charges

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Manchester City found guilty of 114 charges

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.
  • City face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League.
  • If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules. It is a decision that, if upheld, would equate to one of the biggest scandals in football history.

City face a range of sanctions from a fine to points deductions and even expulsion from the Premier League. Or a combination of all, under rule W51 of its handbook. No punishment has yet been announced.

If the verdict is upheld, with City expected to appeal, it will also raise question marks over the 20 trophies the club have won under Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, whose Abu Dhabi group took over in 2008.

The charges can be broken down into five categories and relate to a period from 2009-23 in which City won six League Cups, three FA Cups, seven league titles and the Champions League. There is the provision for removing past titles, but that would appear remote.

City have been the dominant force in English football for most of that time, but that status is under threat with a verdict that will send shockwaves around Europe and could have huge ramifications for the club.

That is unless they can win an appeal, with sources cautioning it still may take up to another two to three years for the case to be resolved, following on from an already five-year investigation.

The Premier League’s rules provide for an independent appeal board with broad powers, including the ability to uphold, vary or overturn the independent commission’s decision.

According to recent reports, it would therefore appear that despite the verdict, the case is far from being resolved and punishment decided. The details of the commission’s findings, when published, will be crucial to determining what happens next.

But if it is upheld, the verdict also opens up the possibility of City facing legal action from other clubs who feel they missed out on trophies and even merit money from league placings.

It is understood Premier League clubs are already discussing legal action and possible compensation claims as a result of the guilty verdict.

Each of those cases would have to be held individually, potentially leading to years more of litigation. Conversely, if City win their appeal, they too could take legal action against the Premier League the damage caused to their reputation.

There has not yet been an official confirmation of the independent panel’s verdict from the Premier League. The Premier League declined to comment.

According to recent reports, however, several sources have told Telegraph Sport that the panel has found City guilty of all but one of the charges they faced. The one that has not been proved is noted to be one of the most serious of the 115.

The damning verdict for City is a major newly introduced test of fragile UK relations with the United Arab Emirates, with whom bilateral trade was worth £25bn last year. Redacted freedom of information documents, seen by Telegraph Sport, show Abu Dhabi hosted UK government officials including Lord Stockwood, then investment minister, as recently as February. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the City chairman and trusted adviser to the UAE president, was present at the meeting. Government notes from the meeting recorded that he “noted they are very proud of what they have achieved through their investments in Manchester”.

Recent findings suggest that the Government previously caused acrimony among senior leaders in Abu Dhabi after putting forward legislation to ban foreign states from owning UK newspapers and news magazines. The intervention prompted the collapse of a takeover of The Telegraph in April 2024, which was largely funded by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the owner of City and vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.

The previous UK government has admitted its embassy in Abu Dhabi and the Foreign Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) in London discussed the charges levelled at City by the Premier League. However it refused to disclose the correspondence.

Industry observers note that city have steadfastly maintained they are innocent, promising “irrefutable” evidence in support of their position, and had assembled some of the most expensive lawyers in the country to argue their case. Despite the verdict, the club are understood to be confident that it will win the argument in the end. Senior figures are noted to be calm about the latest development, as significant as it seems.

In a recent development, city rebuilt their team this summer and it is understood that signings were brought in on conventional player contracts, rather than terms including clauses triggered in the event of a heavy punishment. Given the club have consistently denied breaching financial regulations, and their deals for new players to work with head coach Enzo Maresca underlines their position.

It has been revealed that on Friday, a City spokesman remarked: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such, Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club have diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”.

Sources close to Pep Guardiola, the former City manager who stepped down last summer after 10 years of remarkable success at the club, including a treble triumph in 2023 and an unprecedented fourth straight league title in 2024, insist he has not been informed of any verdict.

In the days after City were first charged, Guardiola mounted a fierce defence of the club, claiming: “I am fully convinced we will be [proved] innocent.”.

The verdict vindicates the Premier League’s decision to launch an investigation after explosive allegations that City had routinely broken financial rules were first made in Der Spiegel in 2018 based on the Football Leaks documents.

Uefa previously accused City of breaches of its financial regulations and announced in 2020 that it was suspending the club from the Champions League for two years for “overstating” sponsorship revenue between 2012 and 2016.

City denied the Uefa charges and, after an appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the two-year ban was overturned. Cas found that a number of the claims brought by Uefa had fallen outside a five-year “time bar” and others were “not established”.

Sources indicate that it did, however, still impose a €10m fine after ruling that City failed to cooperate with investigators. City had previously also agreed a settlement with Uefa of €20m in 2014 following an investigation into their finances.

Legal experts agreed that the commission’s verdict is far from the end of the case. Yasin Patel, barrister at Church Court Chambers, noted: “City’s lawyers will now analyse this decision and look at the options open to them to appeal, which may include procedural impropriety, wrongful interpretation of law, and legal errors – importantly, they can guarantee an appeal.

According to recent reports, “Sanctions could include a major fine, points deduction, relegation or even all three. Factoring in whether titles and trophies should be stripped, whether other clubs have been robbed of further revenue and opportunities due to City’s wrongdoings and losses incurred, we safely say that this is only the first chapter of a long-running legal saga that will not end any time soon.”.

According to recent reports, ian Hargreaves, partner with specialist disputes firm Quillon Law, stated the verdict was “not the end of the story but the beginning of a latest phase”, and added: “There is also the question of whether the panel’s decision can withstand a hard-fought appeal, and on what grounds any challenge might be brought. Much will depend on the detail of the panel’s findings and reasoning, which will inevitably be closely scrutinised by both sides.”.

Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri, who won the Ballon d’Or during his trophy-laden spell at the club, said he believed the club were innocent.

“For the players, it’s different than it is for journalists. I can understand all opinions, but we try to stay positive,” the Spain midfielder said while on international duty.

Recent findings suggest that “When you see all the people who worked hard at City to achieve success, you know what we achieved can’t be taken away. It wasn’t paid for with money, but with effort and teamwork. Everything we achieved was deserved; we marked one of the great eras of English football. I believe in the club’s innocence – we already went through this in 2020.”.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, mentioned: “I think we would all need to study the independent commission’s report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions.”.

Zohran Kwame Mamdani, the mayor of New York, posted “114” in relation to the charges while former Manchester United players David de Gea and Rio Ferdinand both asked whether they should be due winner’s medals from past seasons.

The Premier League statement in February 2023 stated that “a number of alleged breaches” had been referred to an independent commission. It then detailed each specific rule against each season in which the alleged breach took place. The precise number was not clear from the statement and led to varying reports between 115 and 130. Friday’s news suggested the figure was 115.

All the way to 2009-10, the first full season following the club’s takeover by Sheikh Mansour, who is a member of the Abu Dhabi Royal family and the vice president of the United Arab Emirates. There were charges relating to all 14 seasons until the Premier League completed their investigation during the 2022-23 campaign. In that time, City won seven Premier League titles, six League Cups, three FA Cups and the Champions League. They have since won another league title – the first club to do so four times in a row – as well as the Uefa Super Cup, the Fifa Club World Cup and the FA Cup and League Cup double last season.

According to recent reports, they can be split into five groups. The biggest relates to the seasons from 2009-10 until 2017-18 and the requirement for clubs to provide accurate financial information and act in the utmost good faith.

The next set of rules concern the full disclosure of manager and player payments. The alleged manager breaches related to the period between 2009-10 and 2012-13, when Roberto Mancini was leading the team. The alleged breaches with respect to player payments relate to all of the seasons between 2010-11 and 2015-16.

As well as providing financial detail, clubs were required to meet Uefa and Premier League rules which were designed to bring a club’s spending broadly in line with their income by placing set limits on losses. City were charged with breaches of Uefa’s licencing and financial fair play rules from 2013-14 until 2017-18, and the Premier League’s profit and sustainability rules from 2015-16 until 2017-18.

The final set of charges spanned the five seasons during which City were being investigated by the Premier League and rules that require members to cooperate in the utmost good faith by providing information and documents.

A full picture will only emerge when the commission publishes its findings but we know that the Premier League investigation began in December 2018 following allegations in the German newspaper Der Spiegel based on the Football Leaks documents. These included alleged payments to former manager Mancini for consultancy work at an Abu Dhabi-based club that was separate to his regular contract at City.

We also know that City were alleged to have breached rules over setting out image rights payments to players in their club contract. Der Spiegel reported that the Premier League investigation also focused on payments to under-age players, as well as whether club sponsors were paying for commercial deals themselves or a significant proportion was in fact effectively coming from owner Sheikh Mansour.

City have always denied breaking any rules. In response to the Premier League statement about the alleged breaches, they noted that they have “irrefutable evidence” to support their position and “look forward to this matter being put to rest once and for all.”.

Sources indicate that at the start of the hearing in September 2024, Guardiola also said: “Wait for the independent panel. We believe we have not done anything wrong.”.

It’ll be Ben White on the night

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal lads were in action, and on the scoresheet, last night as England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid.
  • Obviously I’m not especially invested in the national sides of other countries, but I was pleased for Ben White after all the nonsense he’s been through with England.
  • Holland was the one who sparked the issue originally when he was working with Gareth Southgate, so hopefully another goal for the Arsenal defender (he got one a few months back I think), and being part of a famous win in Spain will win around some of those fans who were giving him stick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal lads were in action, and on the scoresheet, last night as England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid. Ezri Konsa made it 2-0 with a close range header, Spain might wonder who was marking him (I think it was supposed to be Marc Cucurella) but the movement was really sharp. Then a couple of minute later, Ben White fired England into a 3-0 lead, with Cucurella also in close attendance.

Obviously I’m not especially invested in the national sides of other countries, but I was pleased for Ben White after all the nonsense he’s been through with England. The worst sections of the media have fanned the flames against him, and it doesn’t take much to rile up those who are already of a jingoistic persuasion. As we’ve seen since seen with stories about Steve Holland being hugely unpopular at Man Utd, there’s a common denominator, and it’s not Ben White.

Holland was the one who sparked the issue originally when he was working with Gareth Southgate, so hopefully another goal for the Arsenal defender (he got one a few months back I think), and being part of a famous win in Spain will win around some of those fans who were giving him stick. I also feel quite confident that even if there is a cohort who won’t forgive Ben White for the crime of Steve Holland being a dickhead, he probably won’t care too much. Look at the reactions of his teammates and manager to the goal, and that’s tells you plenty.

According to recent reports, he was also involved in a minor scuffle going off at half-time, which also seemed to involved Konsa and Martin Zubimendi, but I’m sure it was just heat of the moment stuff. Although Spain got two back after England went down to 10 men, they made the fatal mistake of starting Mikel Merino. How was he supposed to come off the bench and get a vital goal then? Silly Luis de la Fuenta, bloke’s a fraud.

Elsewhere over the weekend, Viktor Gyokeres scored twice for Sweden, both from the penalty spot. We just need more penalties. This is the key to unlocking him. Riccardo Calafiori played the full 90 as Italy went down 4-1 to Belgium (ouch), Martin Odegaard played 90 as Norway beat Wales, and there are some more games to come this week with Germany facing Netherlands tonight (Kai v Timber), the Brazilians are in action in Singapore, and apparently Christos Tzolis is fit to play for Greece after having an MRI.

Industry observers note that maybe it’s my own recent experiences, but I don’t care for the idea he needs an MRI. I get it, it’s probably for his knee or hamstring or something, but it feels like if you need one of those to know if you’re fit, you’re probably not feeling 100% anyway. I guess this will be one Mikel Arteta will keep a close eye on tonight when Greece host Serbia and Tzolis inevitably starts. Ideally, these will be useful minutes for him, and help him deliver for us but you can’t help but worry considering he picked up an injury in the last Interlull.

Sources indicate that finally for today, it looks as if a Declan Rice contract extension is close. Speaking while on England duty, he stated:.

Industry observers note that “A fresh contract is hopefully on the horizon soon. I’m extremely lucky to be at a club like Arsenal where the manager reveals me so much trust and teammates who put so much energy and effort into to me.

“I’m extremely lucky not to have to worry about that stuff, and it makes playing football far more easier.”.

This is, by any measure, a no-brainer. I don’t think there’s a club in the world that would turn him down if he were available, and his importance to Arsenal is just obvious. In a world when £100m+ transfers often struggle to provide value, this is one of the exceptions. If you went back to 2023 and had to do it all again, even if you added another £20m or £30m to the fee we paid West Ham, it would be worth it. It’s likely to be the kind of deal that sees him play out the rest of his prime years in red and white, and let’s hope there are more trophies along the way to accompany that.

Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

It has been revealed that the pod should be out around around midday. Until then, have a good one – after which I’m gonna be off for a couple of days but the lads will keep things ticking here until I get back.

By Saikat Mandal | 26 Nov 2026 07:41.

Tottenham Hotspur may have suffered a setback in their pursuit of Inter Milan central midfielder Hakan Calhanoglu ahead of the January transfer window or next summer.

After enduring the worst possible start to the 2026-27 campaign, during which Spurs failed to win any of their opening seven games, they have bounced back strongly in the league.

The north London club have picked up four wins in their last five matches, climbing to 10th in the Premier League table with 15 points, six adrift of fourth-placed Liverpool.

Spurs spent heavily to strengthen their midfield during the summer, bringing in Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes, but the club are still looking to add further quality in that department.

Recent reports have suggested that Tottenham have earmarked Calhanoglu as a target for next summer, although Galatasaray, Juventus and Como are also interested in the midfielder.

According to a report from Football Insider, Spurs may have suffered a blow in the race, with Calhanoglu preferring to remain at Inter Milan.

The 32-year-old midfielder is out of contract with the Italian giants at the end of the season, but preliminary talks have begun over an extension as he is keen to continue his career at San Siro.

Since joining from AC Milan in the summer of 2021, Calhanoglu has scored 53 goals in 226 appearances for the Nerazzurri.

The central midfielder registered 19 goal contributions in 30 games last term and has already scored three goals in his opening 10 league appearances this season.

While Spurs can match Calhanoglu's wage demands, they are not prepared to pay a transfer fee at this stage, instead hoping to sign him on a free transfer.

This leaves Tottenham anxiously waiting to see whether the Turkish midfielder can reach an agreement with Inter over a latest deal.

Calhanoglu can operate as a defensive midfielder and is renowned for his excellent long-range shooting, making him an exciting potential addition to De Zerbi's squad, even at this stage of his career.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s Andrew A covering for Andrew M, who’s playing hooky again. I suppose after 24 years of writing this blog, a few bad habits are bound to creep in….

Recent findings suggest that I’m not going to lie, it’s been a difficult week. Fortunately, a lifetime of watching Arsenal has given me plenty of practice at making bad jokes when I don’t know what else to say.

Sources indicate that it’s either that or tears, and my eye juice reserves are running low after reading just a fraction of the thousands of messages you sent over the weekend. Bluesky, Reddit, X, Discord, Facebook, Patreon. Wherever I looked, there you were, sending love to Blogs. It was beautiful to see.

Recent findings suggest that and to the handful of you who got in touch with me or people I know because you thought Friday’s update was about my health, please hold that thought. I’m fine. Touch wood. There are, in fact, two Andrews at Arseblog, and I’m the other one.

Having been crowned the “World’s Youngest Boy” by James on yesterday’s Arsecast Extra, Max Dowman set yet another record last night, becoming England under-21s’ youngest scorer with the winner in a 3-2 victory over France in filthy conditions in Bristol.

I’d planned to watch from kick-off, but gave up when I realised the game wasn’t on any of the 5,000 channels I pay £150 a month for. Then I saw on social media that Ethan Nwaneri, playing as a number 10, had laid on a couple of goals. So I did the clever thing and googled it. Turns out I needed the official England app and an account. Eyes still rolling, I tried to set up a login, only to find out I already had one. Cue the password reset process, verification codes and me losing the will to live. Just let me watch some fucking children play football in the rain!

In a recent development, by the time I got the stream, it was nearly half-time. At least that gave me a chance to catch up on Nwaneri’s two assists, both of which were Ozil-esque. First he drove down the left and slipped a neat ball inside for Mikey Moore, currently on loan at Cologne, to finish. Then came a teasing dink to the back post that Southampton’s Divin Mubama met first time. Given how little Nwaneri has played for Dortmund lately, it was a welcome reminder of what he can do.

It feels a bit silly to say Max, who was named player of the match, looked comfortable at this level when he’s already got a Premier League winners’ medal next to his GCSE textbooks, but he really did.

Watching him is like reading someone’s really nice handwriting. Even the everyday stuff looks lovely. A touch to bring the ball under control, a little turn, and suddenly the defender who was right up his arse is looking at the back of his shirt. I’ll never get tired of watching him do that.

It has been revealed that as both sides made changes, I expected Lee Carsley to take him off. Instead, he played the full 90 and dug Arsenal teammate Tommy Setford out of a hole. The goalkeeper was at fault for the only goal in Friday’s defeat to Portugal and had another difficult night, spilling a cross into his own net. The rain hardly helped, and the 20-year-old has been doing well on loan at Stevenage, but it was a horrible one to concede.

When Brest’s Giovani Versini whipped in an equaliser with five minutes left, it looked like England would have to settle for a draw, but Dowman’s tap-in settled it with a minute to spare. Who knows, Dowman and Nwaneri could be on the same pitch again next week when Dortmund visit the Emirates.

Elsewhere, Group 2 of League A of the UEFA Nations League (catchy naming scheme, lads) served up another bonkers evening. Jurrien Timber scored twice in the Netherlands’ 7-0 win over Christos Tzolis’ Greece on Friday, only for the Dutch to lose 5-0 to Kai Havertz’s Germany in Berlin. There were some lovely goals from the Germans – including two from Florian Wirtz – who are finding their feet under Jurgen Klopp. Timber and Havertz both came off midway through the second half, seemingly unscathed. Timber’s pride aside, anyway.

Tzolis, meanwhile, was cleared to play after an MRI scan and got through 88 minutes of Greece’s 1-0 win over Serbia. All three sides finished on 11 points, with Germany and the Netherlands going through on goal difference at Greece’s expense.

In a recent development, tonight, Martin Odegaard’s Norway face Denmark, while Viktor Gyokeres will look to extend his record-breaking scoring run for Sweden away at Poland. Piero Hincapie’s Ecuador take on Bolivia, Big Gabi and Bruno are in Singapore with Brazil, and Cristhian Mosquera and Marli Salmon are in action for Spain under-21s and England under-19s, respectively.

Sources indicate that closer to home, The Athletic ran two Arsenal contract stories in quick succession. James reports that Timber has agreed a new long-term deal, while David Ornstein claims Declan Rice’s extension will take him through to 2031. Arsenal already had the option to keep Rice until 2029, so the new deal effectively buys them two more years and gives him a sizeable pay rise for the next four and a half. If he keeps playing as he has been, I can’t imagine many Arsenal fans quibbling with that.

For what it’s worth, we’ve heard on the grapevine that David Raya’s new contract is all but done, too, which means the club are making good progress with the lads whose deals expire in 2028, a list that also includes Odegaard, Havertz, Mikel Merino and our two backup keepers.

It has been revealed that there was an interesting discussion on Arsenal Vision’s ‘Friday Night Clive’ podcast about Arsenal elongating their “winning window” while having one eye on the next iteration of the team. If you hand expensive new contracts to players hurtling towards their thirties, you leave yourself financially exposed and potentially blocking pathways for up-and-coming talent. No doubt the club and manager are keenly aware of that. I just wonder how much you can expect the latter to focus on the faraway future when the dynasty he craves has to start in the here and now.

If this week has taught me anything, it’s that there’s something to be noted for seizing the day. Admittedly, that’s easier when it’s Arsenal’s money I’m volunteering to spend.

If you’re about to part with some of your own (smooth segue, Allen) this year’s Arseblog Christmas Gift Guide is up.

I spent some of last week rounding up Arsenal bits and pieces I’d be happy to find under the tree. Mostly, I wanted to point you towards the independent makers, artists and writers producing stuff I like. In many cases, what I’ve picked is just a small sample of what they do, so have a nose around.

If you’ve got a recommendation of your own, pop the link in the form at the bottom and I’ll take a look.

Right, I’d better crack on with the day job. Lewis is on duty tomorrow and, all being well, Andrew M should be back here before the week is out.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • After Monday’s news that both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice have agreed newly introduced deals with the club, Tuesday brought the news that fellow 2023 signing David Raya was next in line, swiftly followed by reports that Riccardo Calafiori will also be handed a new deal, and Piero Hincapie will be getting improved terms, too.
  • It has been revealed that since the end of the 2024-25 season, there have already been newly introduced deals for Gabriel, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri, William Saliba, Bukayo Saka, and, of course, Mikel Arteta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that good morning! I’ve got to say, if I worked at Arsenal and I wasn’t getting a fresh contract this international break, I think I’d be taking it pretty personally.

After Monday’s news that both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice have agreed newly introduced deals with the club, Tuesday brought the news that fellow 2023 signing David Raya was next in line, swiftly followed by reports that Riccardo Calafiori will also be handed a new deal, and Piero Hincapie will be getting improved terms, too.

It has been revealed that since the end of the 2024-25 season, there have already been newly introduced deals for Gabriel, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri, William Saliba, Bukayo Saka, and, of course, Mikel Arteta. With the latest raft of agreements on top of those, that’s a lot of key people tied down for the next few years.

These deals will mean everyone other than Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Mikel Merino, and Kepa is contracted to the club until at least 2029. That’s a nice feeling, isn’t it? There will be some decisions to be made over a couple of those players and whether it’s time to refresh, you’d imagine, but the bulk of the squad should be staying put and continuing to compete together – with a couple of additions supplementing them, of course – for the next couple of years at least.

Of those four (plus Kepa) mentioned above, you’d have to think Odegaard is the next priority when it comes to renewals, given his importance on and off the pitch and his current form.

I was in a bar here in Berlin catching up with a fellow Arsenal fan yesterday evening (hello, if you’re reading!) and they had Norway’s game in Denmark on. It’s fair to say the skipper continued his fine start to the season.

After Norway went two down against the run of play, Odegaard sprung into action. No player had as many touches on the night, and he was involved in all three Norway goals.

Industry observers note that he stole the ball for the goal that made it 2-1, which, by the way, we should have a word for. We have the word equaliser for when it goes to 2-2, but we don’t have a word for the goal that shortens the lead. The Germans call it an Anschlusstor – literally a ‘connecting goal’, the goal that means the scores are now just one apart.

Recent findings suggest that anyway, Odegaard, pressing as he always does, stole the ball from goalkeeper Mads Hermansen, then selflessly left the tap-in for Erling Haaland. He then scored the equaliser, a goal reminiscent of his opening day strike against Coventry if we’re honest: he didn’t hit it well, he got a bit lucky. But: right place, right time and all that.

Industry observers note that and, finally, it was Odegaard’s ferociously whipped in free-kick that struck the hand of Joachim Andersen and allowed Haaland to convert from the penalty spot late into added time. If you’ve got a few minutes, you can see the highlights of his performance here – some of the touches are more than worth your time.

A good night’s work, especially after he was suffering with a stomach bug last week.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t just the captain in action yesterday, either. Piero Hincapie played just over an hour for Ecuador overnight, there were assists for Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes as Brazil beat Singapore 7-0 earlier on in the day, and then an assist for Viktor Gyokeres too as Sweden drew with Poland.

That looks like something he’s clearly worked on – getting his body in the way of the defender and, rather than holding the ball up, looking to direct it towards an oncoming runner. His assist for Declan Rice in Munich obviously looked pretty similar, and it’s not something we saw too much of last season.

In fact, I thought I’d have a quick look, and Gyokeres has 13 key passes (a pass that leads a shot from a team-mate) in the Premier League and Champions League this season. He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions. It’s hard not to conclude that he’s been working on that side of his game, and these Giroud-esque back-to-goal touches for team-mates are more than welcome.

Recent findings suggest that so, plenty of assists this break. Now we just need to harness that at Newcastle on Saturday and actually have someone to stick the ball in the back of the net at the end of those moves. Thankfully – knock on wood – it seems the players have made it through the break unscathed (there was also another behind-closed-doors appearance for William Saliba – a nod to Tom Canton for that story) and should be raring to go.

Industry observers note that lastly, I want to point you towards Arseblog News, where Andrew A wrote something last night on the death of double-winner Peter Storey, one of just eight players to make over 500 appearances for the club. That first double is such an enormous part of our history wouldn’t have happened without Storey’s nerves of steel in the FA Cup semi-final.

By Saikat Mandal | 26 Nov 2026 08:21.

Manchester United reportedly remain open to selling Marcus Rashford in January if they receive a suitable offer for the forward.

Rashford spent last season on loan at Barcelona, and it appeared that his future lay away from Old Trafford after he fell out with former manager Ruben Amorim.

Man Utd publicly backed his reintegration into the squad after Barcelona opted against signing him permanently, but the England international has so far cut a disappointing figure.

Rashford has made six Premier League appearances this season, starting four of them, but is yet to register a goal or assist.

With Mauricio Pochettino looking to reshape the attacking line-up in his own image, Rashford could once again find himself facing an uncertain future.

Speaking on the Market Madness podcast, transfer expert Ben Jacobs has suggested that the Red Devils would still consider suitable offers for Rashford.

The forward remains under contract at United until 2028, meaning the club are under no immediate pressure to sell him.

At the same time, the Red Devils could consider letting him leave as they look to add depth and quality to their forward department in January or potentially next summer.

Industry observers note that rashford is right now sidelined with a hip injury and missed both of Pochettino's first two games in charge. However, the club expect him to return before the end of the month, potentially in time for the clash against Brentford.

Joshua Zirkzee came on at half-time against Liverpool, but there is a strong possibility that the Dutch striker could be offloaded, with several Serie A clubs reportedly keen on his signature.

Pochettino also needs to reshape his defence, with signing a new centre-back a priority, potentially putting Lisandro Martinez's future at the club in doubt.

There are also doubts over the long-term future of captain Bruno Fernandes, who has already rejected two contract offers from the club.

Gleison Bremer's equaliser earned Juventus a point at the Stadio Artemio Franchi after they twice fell behind against Fiorentina. Spalletti's side now go into the international break outside the Champions League places, with their next home game brought forward by a day.

The point leaves Fiorentina 15th in the table on 9 points.

It has been revealed that the hosts led after four minutes. Mateo Pellegrino scored, set up by Pedro Goncalves. Nick Woltemade levelled in the 32nd minute from a Randal Kolo Muani assist, and it was 1-1 at half-time.

Sources indicate that fiorentina went ahead again in the 54th minute. Guglielmo Vicario made the first save, but the Juventus defenders were too slow to clear. Alieu Njie forced in the rebound. Bremer then reached a Douglas Luiz corner in the six-yard box before David de Gea could get to it.

In a recent development, juventus completed 384 accurate passes to Fiorentina’s 273. Fiorentina still attempted 22 shots to Juventus’s 18, and both sides had 6 on target. The expected goals figures, 2.46 for Juventus and 2.14 for Fiorentina, are consistent with a fairly even contest despite the visitors’ control of the ball.

Recent findings suggest that the closing stages could have gone either way. Former Juventus defender Radu Drăgușin headed in from a corner in the 82nd minute. The goal was ruled out because he pushed Bremer with both hands. Near the end, Vicario saved twice in quick succession to protect the point. Juventus also claimed a penalty when the ball struck João Mário’s arm in the Fiorentina area, but none was given.

In a recent development, referee Andrea Colombo booked three Juventus players. Juan Cabal was cautioned in the 13th minute and Bremer in the 22nd. Kolo Muani was booked for dissent in the 73rd. Christ Inao Oulaï was Fiorentina’s only booking.

Juventus were without the injured Kenan Yildiz, Andrea Cambiaso, Nico González, Manuel Locatelli, Khéphren Thuram and Kamil Grabara. Weston McKennie and Zeki Çelik returned to the squad. Spalletti made three changes in the 57th minute, sending on Zhegrova for Woltemade, Alajbegovic for Boga and Celik for Cabal. Ekhator replaced McKennie in the 78th minute and Gatti came on for Lucumí in the 89th.

At his press conference at the Franchi, Spalletti remarked he was not happy because his team does not play at a steady enough level to aim for anything important. He did praise Kolo Muani, describing him as the player everyone wanted and one he can use as a centre-forward or out wide. Shown a replay of the João Mário incident, he dodged the question and asked, smiling, for a different one.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you.
  • The Interlull is over and that’s it now until March.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you. More the kind where you have three stab wounds in your abdomen and a chunk of your insides taken out. If at all possible, I seriously recommend the former to the latter. Anyway, I’m here right now with coffee and painkillers, which I guess is something akin to Arseblog heritage.

The Interlull is over and that’s it now until March. It’s non-stop Arsenal all the way, and all the focus will be on us and what we can produce on the pitch. For those interested in what our players got up to during this break, and what they delivered for their respective nations, Andrew A has a handy round-up over on Arseblog News. Now it’s about keeping everyone as fit as possible, the manager using the squad in the smartest and most effective way he can, and for some of the players who are capable of producing more doing exactly that.

I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions [PL & CL].

Recent findings suggest that I think sample size might be a factor here, because when you look at his xG per 90, it’s 0.05 per 90 in both Premier League and Champions League this season, versus .99 and .76 per 90 last season, but obviously he played more minutes last time out. After 14 appearances this season, he’s rustled up a total of 614 minutes; this time last season his first 14 appearances brought him a cumulative 1200+ minutes. The absence of Kai Havertz was a factor, obviously, but it was probably that early season load that contributed to the injury he picked up against Burnley after a solid first half performance.

In a recent development, the job for Mikel Arteta is to find a way to share those minutes effectively, to have both his strikers scoring and assisting, and to harness some of what Gyokeres has been able to produce for Sweden. It’s often mooted that as a team we need to play to his strengths more, but perhaps these key pass metrics show that the design is more about eliminating some of the weaknesses in his game to make him more effective in the final third for us. Let’s see how it goes.

Meanwhile, the KMI (Key Match Incident) panel have ruled on the Kai Havertz penalty incident against Hull. They ruled 5-0 that the on-field decision was wrong and that VAR, manned that day by Michael Oliver, should have intervened:.

According to recent reports, although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz. Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded.

Recent findings suggest that I get every day is a learning day for ‘ProRef’, the people whose job it is to know the rules of football but week after week seem to demonstrate in upcoming and inventive ways that they don’t. The question for us as fans is, what are we supposed to do with this? Are we supposed to feel better knowing that they’re owning up to mistakes? It feels a bit like getting run over when you have the green light at a pedestrian crossing, a nearby cop just lets the bloke go, but then later a judge claims he should have been stopped and arrested.

It has been revealed that which is all well and good when you’re in a hospital bed in traction with a couple of broken legs and smashed pelvis (I say this only because I remember being in hospital with a bloke who fell under a bus and that’s what happened to him. He was fine though, his mates brought him in loads of joints which he used to share in the smoking room – this was 90s hospital). Which is to say, the damage has been done, the admission the bloke got it wrong in the first place doesn’t really make you feel any better.

It has been revealed that from our perspective at least, Martin Odegaard’s winner ensured that decision didn’t turn out to be one which went on to live in infamy – like not drawing the lines for that Brentford goal that time, but it’s still essentially useless. Not least because you just know this weekend or next weekend some other mad thing will happen and they’ll say ‘Oooops! Sorry about that LOL here’s Michael Owen and Howard Webb!’, and some team will lose points because they can’t properly apply the rules of the game to things that happen on the pitch.

According to recent reports, finally for today, we’re being linked with a January move for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott. He’s certainly a fine player, but it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me given we already have the best midfield depth in the Premier League, and beyond. Where does he fit with Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Martin Odegaard? Perhaps if, for example, Zubi went there’s a case to be made for a replacement, but as it is he’s struggling for minutes anyway, and you don’t pay that kind of money for someone to come in and be peripheral.

In a recent development, like most of you, if there’s money to be spent in January, I’d much rather see it go on the forward line where I feel like there’s obvious room for improvement and to increase our depth. The left hand side is the obvious place, it’s hard not to worry about the right a little bit with Bukayo Saka’s injury, and the striker conversation is one which is never quite going to go away. So, on that basis, links to Scott don’t really add up for me. Unless Arteta fancies converting him to another left-back. Then it all clicks, but I think there’s one Bournemouth player we’d all rather see arrive.

Right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. In terms of a podcast, I’m not quite feeling up to it today, but what we’ll do is make our Patreon preview podcast free and available to everyone tomorrow afternoon. I should be less sore then, and I continue to be blown away by your many emails and messages. Thank you so much, they mean the world.

Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb.

“It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play,” McBurnie told BBC Scotland.

“We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored. I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

Recent findings suggest that “Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

However, the goal that would have made the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager’s debut as an international boss more memorable ultimately failed to arrive.

In this extended international break, the Scots will host Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday and then travel to North Macedonia before taking on Slovenia in Glasgow, with the Tartan Army hoping to see further improvement – and goals.

September 29: Scotland vs Switzerland.

October 3: North Macedonia vs Scotland.

October 6: Scotland vs Slovenia.

November 13: Scotland vs North Macedonia.

November 16: Switzerland vs Scotland.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, the debutant mentioned: “Thought we struggled to get into the game first half, but second half we completely dominated the game.

It has been revealed that “They’ve got a top goalie who made really good saves. So many positives to take and a clean sheet as well.

“We changed shape a wee bit at half-time to get more control and that did really well for us.

“It’s a substantial game again on Tuesday so it’s key to recover now and go again.

“I’ve played on the left-hand side for a couple of years now, so I’m comfortable doing that.

Recent findings suggest that “We’ve had a great week. A new manager, new way of playing and new faces in camp. It’s just the chances we need to take - the fact we’re creating the chances stands us in good stead.”.

The striker told BBC Scotland: “It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play.

Recent findings suggest that “We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored.

“I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

According to recent reports, “Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

Pocognoli’s first game in charge of Scotland ends in a goalless draw. The visitors produced a dominant second-half display, but their final ball and end-product was severely lacking in crucial moments. Ure, Hickey, Gilmour, McBurnie and Bowie all came close to scoring, but no one could break the deadlock.

Scotland cannot find a way past the impenetrable Oblak. There will be just two minutes of added time for the visitors to possibly score a late winner.

Lovric clatters into Gilmour and is cautioned. Slovenia can’t get out. It’s wave after wave of Scottish pressure.

Oblak comes out and fails to claim Robertson’s free-kick. The ball is recycled and the Tottenham full-back whips a second cross into the box and Slovenia fail to clear. Welsh is waiting for it, but lashes a first-time volley over the bar.

Karnicnik catches Robertson with a late lunging tackle and receives a yellow card, giving Scotland a chance to get the ball into the box.

The hosts make their fifth alteration of the afternoon, with Cerin withdrawn and Lovric on instead.

How has Bowie missed?! Gilmour finds Bowie with an outstanding pass through the centre of Slovenia’s defence. The substitute takes a touch then scuffs a rushed finish wide. Bowie has to do better there!

Another change is here for Scotland, with Gannon-Doak on to replace Hickey.

It has been revealed that welsh spots Bowie’s run and threads a perfectly-weighted pass through to the forward. From an unfavourable angle, the substitute’s one-on-one attempt is blocked by Oblak.

Pocognoli orders Scotland’s first alteration of the game, with Bowie replacing Ure up top.

On paper, it looks like Sebastien Pocognoli has opted for a five-back formation, with Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh making his Scotland debut as one of the centre backs.

Captain Andy Robertson and Brentford’s Aaron Hickey will operate as the wing-backs, with Billy Gilmour, Lewis Ferguson and John McGinn forming a midfield three.

A newly introduced-look attack is spearheaded by the returning Oli McBurnie and 22-year-old Robbie Ure, who like Welsh, will also make his Scotland debut.

Angus Gunn remains his country’s first-choice goalkeeper.

Debutants Robbie Ure and Stephen Welsh are each poised for their first international cap. Billy Gilmour returns to the starting XI after missing the World Cup through injury and Oli McBurnie will make his first appearance for Scotland since 2021.

“The first game is always a special game so you have to bring the mental aspect in for the players and for the staff.

It has been revealed that “A good result can help but the most important thing is we see things that we work on through the week. I hope is we apply that well then we will get the result which will be the perfect mix.

“I hope we can bring a good game, and a good exciting principle on the pitch. I think we need the support from the supporters because there’s a lot of latest players.

In a recent development, “We need to create a good energy but it’s up to us on the pitch to create this. So then we can be hand in hand with the supporters.”.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

Scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his upcoming role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

Process of Elimination

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through.
  • According to recent reports, arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight.
  • Industry observers note that in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapie are all reportedly on the verge of latest deals, with Riccardo Calafiori’s deal also in the in-tray for Andrea Berta too.

According to recent reports, arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight. Back in the summer of 2021, the club enacted a policy of buying players under 24 years old. I always felt like this was the true year zero of the Arteta project. That always felt like the window that built the foundations.

Industry observers note that in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since. Emile Smith Rowe also signed a new contract and took the number 10 shirt that summer and now he is scratching around for minutes at Fulham.

The summer of 2022 saw the arrivals of Gabriel Jesus and Alex Zinchenko, as well as Fabio Vieira. The former pair briefly elevated Arsenal to a upcoming level before becoming promptly obsolete. Vieira was a fairly pricey gamble that didn’t pay off. It was the summer of 2023 that truly established Arsenal among England’s elite. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Kai Havertz’s arrivals turned Arsenal from caterpillars to butterflies.

According to recent reports, three of those players are about to sign latest contracts. Curiously, we have little to no reporting on whether Kai Havertz is lined up for a new deal as yet. Arsenal are banking on their well assembled core to deliver more silverware as they enter their peak years (Raya is 31 which feels close to peak age for a goalkeeper).

Undoubtedly, there are some players who will drift away in the coming years. Mikel Merino, Martin Zubimendi and Ben White feel unlikely to get latest Arsenal contracts at this particular moment in time. (Though these things can and do change). Like Havertz, Odegaard’s deal runs until the summer of 2028 and we have yet to hear rumblings of a new deal.

Industry observers note that odegaard and Havertz have negotiated significant fitness challenges over the last two seasons, which probably explains why they have found themselves lower down Berta’s to do list. Timber has had his own physical challenges too, but he is 25. Havertz and Odegaard are 27. Their next contracts will be their last ‘massive’ contracts in terms of wages and their resale value will drop to close to zero if Arsenal tie them down. It makes sense for the club to take its time a little more with both players.

According to recent reports, both are also defining attacking and / or creative players in the Arsenal team. At some point, Arteta is going to have to plot an evolution within this core and it feels like that is more likely to happen in the final third of the pitch than within the core of players who operate behind the ball. Behind the ball, Arsenal are absolutely tip top and have some of the most elite players in the world in their positions.

That is not as true ahead of the ball. Odegaard and Havertz remain, for my money, elite, defining players for Arsenal. For the purposes of this piece; I am going to speculate that Odegaard is going to be offered a new contract given his status in the team and because his role is a little more holistic and he doesn’t solely operate in the final third.

Which leaves us with Havertz. I rate Havertz really highly and believe he is integral to Arsenal’s style, he has the technical quality to play one touch football and the physical quality to act as a release valve and hold the ball up. I can’t think of many forwards who offer both sides of the game to such an extent.

Sources indicate that there are several Arsenal attackers I would trade in before Havertz. However, the market doesn’t always bend to your will. Arsenal remain a self sustaining club and in the PSR / SCR era, player trading has never been more vital or more voluminous. Keeping money swishing between the cost and revenue columns is a necessity in this environment.

It has been revealed that clearly, the number one impediment to Havertz getting a new deal is his fitness. He is still clearly preferred by the manager to Viktor Gyokeres. I have to say I am surprised (a little unpleasantly) at how promptly the tide of opinion has turned against Havertz. The run he went on very recently that saw him score in the Champions League Final, score the goal that clinched the title against Burnley, a critical goal against Chelsea and the winning goal at Anfield seem to have just bought him absolutely no credit within the fan base, which I find a little surprising.

However, Arsenal need to boost their attacking prowess overall at some point very soon. Like I mentioned, I would consider Havertz a superior player to all of Eze, Gyokeres, Tzolis and Madueke. The squad is well served for numbers in attack; it doesn’t have any gaps in that respect. It has a gap in elite quality.

Recent findings suggest that the key to boosting that might not be ‘who is the least effective player?’ it might be ‘who is the most saleable?’ Sometimes you do just have to cash in your chips on a player to evolve and move forwards. It doesn’t always have to be because the player is obsolete or not good enough. Arsenal have such numbers in midfield that there also isn’t really a route into the team there for Havertz either.

Recent findings suggest that if someone offered £60-70m for Gyokeres or Eze, I would accept it and give Havertz a new contract the next day (assuming he does prove his fitness). But I think those scenarios are unlikely. I am not arguing that we have definitely reached the ‘we must sell Kai’ stage and I will reiterate that, at this moment in time, I consider him a very key player who should pretty much always start when fit.

Industry observers note that while he isn’t the most prolific finisher as a centre-forward, crucial goals this season against Chelsea and Liverpool demonstrate his worth. The conversation about moving on only becomes live on condition that the money is used to immediately buy an obviously elite attacker- preferably a centre-forward in that case since that is the gap a Havertz departure would leave.

Industry observers note that but I am certain it is a conversation Arteta and Andrea Berta are currently entertaining. Arteta will want to push the level of the team even further and, to fund what that is going to entail, potentially painful sales will have to be made somewhere. The vigour with which the club pursued the sale of Gabriel Martinelli this summer indicates the manager has the stomach for that conversation too.

#197937. Tech Report: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5192 w)

Tech Report: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Modern and future electronics harbour a key challenge: as conventional metal wires shrink to nanoscale dimensions, their resistivity increases sharply1 owing to surface and grain-boundary scattering. To circumvent this unwanted behaviour, here, we explore the fundamental limits of charge transport in topological semimetal niobium phosphide (NbP) nanoribbons down to approximately 6-nm widths, with industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication. The extracted NbP nanoribbon resistivity reaches 18 ± 4.1 μΩ cm at room temperature with an approximately 9-nm2 cross-sectional area, lower than that of conventional metals and semimetals with comparable size. The NbP nanoribbon resistivity decreases with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper. This trend suggests a growing relative contribution of surface and edge states as the nanoribbon cross-section is reduced, despite a certain amount of disorder, including edge roughness. Our findings advance the understanding of size-dependent transport and scaling in this class of semimetals, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects in future nanoelectronics.
