💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, taking on Borussia Dortmund at home.
  • He’s not fit for tomorrow, unfortunately, but it doesn’t look too serious.
  • Industry observers note that we expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain that he had at that moment, and the first test that we’ve done showed something that is much more encouraging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, taking on Borussia Dortmund at home. It’s a game that Kepa Arrizabalaga will start in the absence of David Raya, but the news around the Arsenal number 1 was a little more positive than expected. In his press conference yesterday, Mikel Arteta said:.

He’s not fit for tomorrow, unfortunately, but it doesn’t look too serious. We need some more tests tomorrow, but it’s quite encouraging. With the pain that he was showing immediately after the action, we were all quite worried, but he seems to be better than what we expected.

Industry observers note that we expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain that he had at that moment, and the first test that we’ve done showed something that is much more encouraging. There’s no need for surgery, which was the main fear especially because that would rule him out for months, so let’s see.

Sources indicate that so, it seems like he’s going to miss a few games, but not anything prolonged, which is obviously good news. Elsewhere, there’s room for rotation, and I think this might be a good chance to give minutes to William Saliba who hasn’t played competitively since the World Cup. He’s had a couple of behind closed doors appearances, which will be useful in terms of fitness, but nothing compares with actually playing at this level.

It has been revealed that I wonder too if players like Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie will fancy their chances, but that seems like a lot of change in the back four – and the goalkeeper – so we’ll have to wait and see there. In midfield, we can bring Myles Lewis-Skelly in for a start, but obviously the manager has plenty to choose from in there, and up front I imagine it will be a chance for Viktor Gyokeres whose minutes have been scant so far this season. Asked if the striker had been knocking on his door about that, Arteta mentioned:.

No, we have conversations with every player to make sure that they understand what we are doing, to gather information about the way they are feeling, and so far, it’s been very positive with Viktor and with the rest of the team.

He could really use a goal tonight if he does start, as does Christos Tzolis whose numbers so far this season aren’t where you’d like them to be. Obviously there’s more to assessing a player than simply goals and assists, but for a left winger brought into replace two players who contributed a lot to the team over the last few seasons, just two assists from 11 appearances (Community Shield excluded) is a little below what you’d hope. He has had an injury, of course, but if his season needs a kick-start, tonight would be very timely.

According to recent reports, dortmund sit top of the Bundesliga right now, unbeaten in the league thus far, and with just one defeat all season in all competitions. That did come in the Champions League, away to Bodo Glimt, but this will be a tricky test tonight for Arsenal. Arteta claims:.

I’m very impressed with them, you see the results so far, where they are in the Bundesliga at the top and where they are in the Champions League and especially the way they are playing, the way they are dominating games, the amount of threat they are able to create. We had them here in pre-season, and they indicated the quality and what they are capable of, so we are very much aware of that. But we play at home in front of our crowd, and now we’re going to go and attack the game, that’s for sure.

After a disappointing second half against Newcastle on Saturday, I’m sure the manager will be looking for a response from his side. It’s nice to be at home again, and a long spell of games in London will hopefully less taxing physically without all the travel, so it’d be good to get that off to a winning start tonight.

Elsewhere, Bruno Guimaraes spoke about his first few months at the club, and how he now feels like he’s getting to grips with what Mikel Arteta wants from him, saying:.

Recent findings suggest that I’m here, I don’t know, three, four months? It’s still a lot to go, but I now definitely understand my role in the team, the way that Mikel wants me to play in the team. So, yeah, I think I still can play much, much better.

Sources indicate that and it’s quite interesting to hear him talk about how at Arsenal he is more ‘free’ than he was under Eddie Howe at Newcastle. Most would feel it was the other way around, but he explained:.

It’s very different. When I was at Newcastle, you play more positional, keep more your position. Here it’s a little bit more free.

If you see the game against Newcastle, they were marking us man to man. You see JT [Jurrien Timber] plays a six, an eight and a number nine sometimes, so you have to move a lot. Of course, I was not used to it. So now I understand a little bit more what he wants for the midfield.

According to recent reports, I think there’s more to come from him, he’s looked good at times, a little off the pace at others, and I think my main worry is about the physical side of his game. Does he have the running power and athleticism that enables players like Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard to thrive under this manager? At 29, he’s no spring chicken, but I guess there’s always room for improvement. Anyway, his press conference stuff from yesterday is worth reading, and there’s some good chat about him on the Arsecast Extra which you’ll find below.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. As ever, we’ll bring you live blog coverage of the game later, as well all the post-game stuff on Arseblog News like the match report, player ratings, manager reaction, quotes round-up and more. #197917. Industry News: Arsenal 1-1 Dortmund: Familiar flaws hold Arsenal back

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1729 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arseblog ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Arsenal 1-1 Dortmund: Familiar flaws hold Arsenal back

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday raised some very familiar concerns and, if we’re being honest, revealed nothing we didn’t already know.
  • It has been revealed that arsenal can play world-class football and completely dominate teams for long spells, but lack the world-class attack to make the most of that domination, the sort of players you just know will create and convert big chances when the time comes.
  • Sources indicate that I really feel like I could write two versions of today’s blog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday raised some very familiar concerns and, if we’re being honest, revealed nothing we didn’t already know.

It has been revealed that arsenal can play world-class football and completely dominate teams for long spells, but lack the world-class attack to make the most of that domination, the sort of players you just know will create and convert big chances when the time comes. And the way the team is starting games after the break is worrying, with teams who are battered to within an inch of their lives early on suddenly able to compete.

Sources indicate that I really feel like I could write two versions of today’s blog. One where I’m miserable, of course: the players can’t shoot, they make all the wrong choices in the decisive moment, we can’t keep wasting chances and dropping off after the break, if Andrea Berta doesn’t deliver the true heirs to Thierry Henry and Robert Pires in January, then he should be stuffed into one of the cannons outside the Armoury and fired into the cold night air.

The other version is much more glass half full: Arteta is coaching masterclasses every week, this level of dominance in games is something I could only dream of a few years ago, that’s the most shots we’ve had in a game all season, we’re top of the league, we’re creating loads without any set-piece reliance and without Bukayo Saka – the goals will come.

Some people reading this would prefer (and relate better to) one version, and others the other version, I’m sure. Let’s see where we end up!

There were, as there tends to be in these Champions League games, a fair few changes from the weekend. Kepa, Piero Hincapie, Ben White, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Christos Tzolis, and Viktor Gyokeres all came into the team.

Despite featuring half a different side, there were plenty of parallels with the Newcastle match. Arsenal were dominant from the off, with Hincapie and White taking turns to play off of Gyokeres. Dortmund had no idea how to cover them and both fullbacks were the targets of early crosses into the box.

Industry observers note that after a couple of long-range efforts, Arsenal got their goal they deserved, with Gyokeres launching a ferocious, dipping effort beyond Gregor Kobel. The Swede can put his foot through the ball, that’s for sure, and the Dortmund backline gave him the sort of time and space to set himself that he doesn’t often get.

The pressure continued after the opener for a while, with Tzolis forcing a good save and Madueke just unable to sort his feet to tap in the rebound.

It has been revealed that it’s fair to say the game settled down after 15/20 minutes, with Dortmund growing into it a little, but it was still Arsenal who looked like scoring the next goal. Rice shot over from almost the same patch of grass Gyokeres had scored from, and the midfielder had another chance when a beautiful one-touch move ended with him bursting through, hurtling towards the Dortmund box. Maybe he could’ve picked out Madueke in support, but he went alone and Nico Schlotterbeck just got across to block the shot.

In a recent development, another huge chance was denied by the offside flag as much as the finishing – Madueke won the ball high, Odegaard squared it to Gyokeres, and the Swede fired over from near the penalty spot. Odegaard was ruled offside but I’m not convinced: had the ball hit the net, I think we’d have seen a very tight VAR check.

Industry observers note that there was one thought on everyone’s minds at half-time: don’t do the same thing again. After Slavia Prague and Newcastle, do not do the same thing again.

Arsenal did the same thing again.

Gyokeres was, by UEFA standards, lucky not to concede a penalty when a corner struck him on the arm. There was another early warning sign with Dortmund sliding the ball across the box and Maximilian Beier kicking the air. He didn’t make the same mistake with his next opportunity. Centre-back Joane Gadou (who was very impressive all evening) charged through the heart of the pitch before playing the ball to Beier, who jinked to unbalance Gabriel and slotted home.

It has been revealed that sometimes a goal is just a good goal, and I don’t think anyone was really at fault here. It’s a great run from Gadou, Beier tricks Gabriel to take the ball onto his weaker left side – it’s fair if Gabriel is expecting (and blocking the angle) on the attacker’s favoured foot, I know how that can happen. I think if we score that goal we’re talking about two brilliant individuals, rather than defensive errors.

My first thought? Not again. My second? OK, how do we respond? Because on Saturday, the response was poor.

Industry observers note that this time it was a lot better. Jobe Bellingham had a rebound disallowed for offside, a moment that really brought the crowd back into the game, but in truth, that was Dortmund’s only real moment of threat. From the goal on 55 minutes to full-time, Arsenal had 15 shots to Dortmund’s two.

And that doesn’t include Serhou Guirassy playing one-twos with the post after a clever, low free-kick from Martin Odegaard late on.

Industry observers note that madueke had an effort blocked. Gyokeres flicked a header wide. Madueke shot wide beyond the far post after a good run. Gyokeres missed a big chance with his head from six yards out. Rice hit the near post from a tight angle after a brilliant pass from Eberechi Eze.

A couple of late corners came to nothing, and that was it.

Mikel Arteta was clearly pleased with the performance on the whole:.

Industry observers note that well, I think I love the way the team played. There’s no question how superior, how dominant, how much of a threat we were, how connected everybody was to the game … It was great to watch. It was unbelievable that sometimes the ball hasn’t ended up in the back of the net. That’s my feeling.

to do what we’ve done out there is just something to be very, very pleased about, because there is very little more that we can demand from the team.

But we all know what that little more is:.

obviously the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance, the amount of chances, the situation, and even shots that are not there. We are three against two, two against one, and the ball doesn’t land with the right person. There is an element of luck, there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist, because I think what the team has done and shown today is the right direction.

Often when Arsenal don’t win games, it feels like it’s because the team haven’t created enough chances. We end up focusing on that one moment, where that one player didn’t execute the way you wanted. But last night wasn’t one of those: Arsenal didn’t struggle to turn dominance into good, slick football, and that football into a healthy number of decent opportunities.

Recent findings suggest that that’s incredibly frustrating, but I do think you win a lot more often than not when you do that. Maybe that’s a hard sell for some this morning, but it’s how I feel about it when we play well, especially when we’ve been winning games anyway. That’s the first time this season we’ve gone two without a win across all competitions, and we’ve won 14 of 19 games so far. Sometimes things don’t fall for you, and this one felt a lot like ‘one of those’, certainly more than Newcastle did.

A word for a couple of promising performances too, with the boss asked about Gyokeres in his post-match press conference:.

Industry observers note that what I love the most is how connected he was to the team. We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threw it in behind and stretched the pitch. There was a lot to like in that performance and that’s the victory that we need.

His finishing was off after the brilliant opener, but at least he was in the positions: too often this season and last, Gyokeres has gone through a game barely registering a shot. He had seven last night, and if he can do that more often he’ll score a lot more. His general play was improved too, both holding the ball up and competing in behind.

Industry observers note that and I thought Martin Odegaard was excellent too. His eight chances created from open play was the most of any player in any Champions League match so far this season.

Since we returned to the competition in 2023, we’ve had a player create more than five chances in a match just twice: Odegaard at Napoli in September (6) and Odegaard last night (9). He’s incredibly unlucky not to be leaving the game with a couple of assists.

Sources indicate that the draw leaves us in a decent position to finish in the all-important top eight in the league phase still, although you have to squint a bit to see us landing in the also-important top two. Real Madrid are up next and that’s a reminder of the sort of teams we’re up against: finishing in the top two is a tall order at the best of times.

With each passing game, it is impossible not to wonder what could be done in January to add to the team. Unless there’s a sudden uptick out of nowhere, those thoughts aren’t disappearing. And even if there is a massive uptick, those thoughts will still be around. But 30 shots is the most we’ve had in a game all season, and the same group of players have scored more goals with fewer shots (/chances) plenty of times. Let’s hope we see some more clinical finishing on Sunday.

Guess I landed on the glass half full version.

There should be an Arsecast once Blogs has caught up with the game, so stay tuned for that. Enjoy your Wednesdays!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that serie A's sporting judge fined Juventus for holding up the start of the game at Fiorentina, and handed the hosts the same penalty.
  • Recent findings suggest that juventus came out of their trip to Florence with a bill rather than a ban.
  • The rulings came in Official Communiqué No.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that serie A's sporting judge fined Juventus for holding up the start of the game at Fiorentina, and handed the hosts the same penalty. No Juventus player is banned, so Spalletti has a full squad for Venezia, though Bremer and Kolo Muani now have a sanction against their names.

Recent findings suggest that juventus came out of their trip to Florence with a bill rather than a ban. Serie A sporting judge Gerardo Mastrandrea punished the club for an unjustified delay to the start of the first half at Fiorentina. The hosts were handed an identical penalty for the same hold-up.

The rulings came in Official Communiqué No. 60, published in Milan on 10 November 2026. Mastrandrea reached them at a meeting that day with Stefania Ginesio and AIA referees’ representative Carlo Moretti. The communiqué states that the fines, including those given to individual club members, will be charged to each club’s LCA league account.

According to recent reports, only one club paid more than Juventus. Como received the heaviest club fine of the round, €10,000, for delaying the start of the second half by about two minutes. The judge treated that as a repeated offence. Genoa were fined €4,000 and Lazio €3,000.

According to recent reports, more notable for Spalletti is what the ruling did not contain. No Juventus player was suspended. Only two players across the league were banned after round 11, according to Corriere dello Sport. They were Parma’s Ndiaye and Frosinone’s Bracaglia, each for one match.

That leaves Spalletti with a full squad for the first game after the international break. He will want every option. The match in Florence, scheduled for Sunday 8 November at 20:45, was assigned to referee Colombo, with Maresca as fourth official and Di Paolo on VAR.

Sources indicate that it ended in a draw that left Juventus seventh on 18 points, Eurosport reported. Fiorentina stayed two points clear of the relegation zone. Spalletti remarked afterwards that his side “are not consistent” and sometimes lose their way over very little.

Recent findings suggest that the ruling did leave a mark on four first-team figures. Randal Kolo Muani, Gleison Bremer and Juan Cabal each picked up their first sanction of the season. Spalletti’s assistant Marco Domenichini did too.

Bremer and Kolo Muani are key players for the coach.

According to recent reports, the count has only started, but it will matter as the season goes on. The fine itself is small, and the sporting picture is unchanged.

Juventus host Venezia at the Allianz Stadium on Sunday 22 November at 12:30.

  • TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thomas Tuchel has never been inclined to place much faith in the most famous right-back at his disposal, Trent Alexander-Arnold, once of Liverpool, now of Real Madrid, and – back in an England shirt – still capable of changing games in the blink of an eye.

England always looked likely to defeat a beleaguered Czech Republic team down to 10 men with just 25 minutes played, but it still required one man to conjure the moment of inspiration in this Nations League tie. This was the first cap in 15 months for the right-back now known simply as “Trent” in an England shirt – as well as his Real Madrid jersey – rather than the six syllables of his surname. With the game level at half-time, two minutes into the fresh half, he twice won the ball before landing a cross on the head of Anthony Gordon for the first goal.

TRENT ➡️ GORDON ⚽️🔥Anthony Gordon can't stop scoring for England, 3 goals in his last 3 games for England 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿#ITVFootball | @England pic.twitter.com/xmqPIULJ24.

Sources indicate that will the Alexander-Arnold with England experiment survive? One feels that Tuchel will need a little more to convince him to abandon whatever reservations he has about the Liverpudlian. A week short of his 28th birthday, Alexander-Arnold was winning just his 35th cap. His Real Madrid team-mate Jude Bellingham, a second-half substitute, was earning his 58th cap less than two months after his 23rd birthday. Thomas Tuchel has backed Jude Bellingham as a future England captain after giving him the armband in the victory over the Czech Republic.

In the absence of Declan Rice, who was vice-captain at the World Cup, Bellingham assumed the role when he came on for Harry Kane, who is now in his 10th season as England captain and also scored in the 2-0 win in Prague.

Tuchel, who needs to check on Bellingham ahead of Saturday’s game against Croatia after a “niggle,” has praised the midfielder’s attitude during the extended international break one year after he was back from an injury but left out of the squad.

“If you are the captain at the end of these matches, you can be the permanent captain,” Tuchel said when asked whether Bellingham could eventually lead the team. “He was the captain against New Zealand before the World Cup. It is always a reward and always an honour.

According to recent reports, “I think he loves to be with us at the moment. That’s what I feel, and we had this small talk today about his role. We felt in our hearts or our stomachs to say ‘let’s go again, let’s start again’ and also our heads told us maybe 30 minutes is enough for this match because he hasn’t played in this quick turnaround through this season. He has done it before, but not in the season, so we didn’t want to be the first ones to try that.

“But even in this little encounter, you can see that he’s confident and happy to help from the bench. So it’s a reward. It’s good. He had a little niggle at the end of the match, so hopefully it’s nothing serious, and he’s available for Croatia.”.

Nico O’Reilly is a doubt for the Croatia match in Rijeka and there are also concerns over Ezri Konsa, who was on the bench but not fit enough to play.

Trent Alexander-Arnold provided an assist for Anthony Gordon in the Real Madrid full-back’s first cap in 15 months. Gordon, meanwhile, has now scored in the first two Nations League games of the campaign and is staking his case to be an indispensable player for Tuchel.

“He’s getting there. He’s defending his shirt, he’s defending his position, an excellent performance again after his performance against Spain,” Tuchel said.

“He was very decisive today and had an excellent goal. It was very, very difficult, but the technique and finishing was excellent. He scored against Spain, so he has decisive actions and he’s defending his shirt and his position. He does it on the highest level and he’s a very key player.”.

The Professional Footballers’ Association has leapt to Cole Palmer’s defence following his withdrawal from the England squad.

The union’s CEO,  Maheta Molango, stated the Chelsea forward is a victim of a “sick” system that is demanding too much from players physically.

“When England see five players who need to withdraw when the single most proud moment a player has is to be called up for the national team, you just ask yourself, what’s wrong about the industry?” Molango said at the Fifpro performance summit in London.

“You see people like Cole Palmer, someone who would have played four consecutive summers in a row had he gone to the World Cup, and you wonder why is he missing?”He’s missing because he’s a victim of the calendar and that’s something that needs to absolutely trigger the alarm bells.”.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is in line to make his first England start under head coach Thomas Tuchel for tonight’s Nations League game against Czech Republic.

Injuries to Nico O’Reilly and Ezri Konsa have forced Tuchel into changes at the back, with Alexander-Arnold expected to come in at right-back, Trevoh Chalobah to replace Konsa and Lewis Hall to step in for O’Reilly.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges related to “serious breaches” of the league’s financial rules, with the commission also upholding all but one in relation to their failure to co-operate with an investigation spanning over three years.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that thanks to Lewis for taking care of the blog yesterday as I was unable to watch the Borussia Dortmund match live.
  • I think while I have some frustrations overall with our inability to turn dominance into goals, I’m more comfortable with it when we’re actually making chances.
  • Sources indicate that it wasn’t that long ago that it was the other way around.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that thanks to Lewis for taking care of the blog yesterday as I was unable to watch the Borussia Dortmund match live. I saw that we’d scored early but only saw the final score well after the full-time whistle, so I guess it was a little disappointing not to have built on that fantastic hit from Viktor Gyokeres.

I think while I have some frustrations overall with our inability to turn dominance into goals, I’m more comfortable with it when we’re actually making chances. I think the manager would have a far bigger problem on his hands if we weren’t, and on Tuesday night the fact we had 30 attempts on goal tells you the problem isn’t chance creation, it’s about being clinical.

Sources indicate that it wasn’t that long ago that it was the other way around. We found it hard to make goalscoring opportunities and for me that’s much more of a worry. It doesn’t mean we can’t improve, it doesn’t mean January becomes any less important the closer it gets, it’s just that the solution lies with the players we have who should be capable of better. There were a couple of other opportunities for Gyokeres that could easily have made this a better night for him and for Arsenal, Declan Rice hit the post, fine margins that shouldn’t be impossible to squeeze in our favour. Make ’em wider, thicker.

Sources indicate that in the end though, I think the bottom line is quality of personnel. Over the last few seasons the only front three player we’ve had who looked like he could become top, top quality was Bukayo Saka. He was certainly on that trajectory until injuries became a real hindrance, and we saw that this season there were modifications made to his game to make him more effective. I know the discourse around him was a little polarised, but I saw a player more involved, who looked sharper and capable of producing the kind of volume that made him so impactful.

Saka isn’t one of those who finishes every chance he gets, he’s a guy who just keeps going until he makes something happen. The hamstring injury, and then the ongoing Achilles issue made it harder for him to contribute, but I really was encouraged by his season until the injury he sustained against Bayern. And it’s interesting to me that while it might be the kind of player he is anyway, we’ve basically asked Noni Madueke to replicate ‘Old Saka’ in terms of that kind of volume of shots and crosses. He’s had 11 shots across the last two games, and perhaps a single goal from those appear to be a scant return, I think it’s how we need him to play and how Arsenal can maximise what we’ve got up front.

It has been revealed that there was an interesting comment on the Arses yesterday wondering how it is that Mikel Arteta can coach and improve defenders and midfielders so well, but not do the same with his attacking players. Some will say it’s because he’s a coach who is defensively minded and this is his wheelhouse. This is what he’s good at. Make a great defence, build a solid midfield in front of them. Perhaps there’s an element of truth in that, but for me it’s down to the players he has to work with.

It has been revealed that if the raw ingredients are good, the recipe has a much better chance of being good, regardless of the talent of the chef. If you get to work with players like Ben White, William Saliba, Gabriel, Riccardo Calafiori, Declan Rice, Martin Odegaard etc, all of whom arrived in at a relatively young age (Rice perhaps the exception because he had a lot of experience, but Arteta has still made him better), you can develop that potential, build relationships, and see that come to fruition on the pitch.

Sources indicate that up front though, I don’t think we’ve had that level of talent. What can you do with a Willian or a Marquinhos? What can you do with a Gabriel Jesus whose knee explodes (perhaps as we saw in those opening few months before injury hit, you could have done a lot more)? Was Gabriel Martinelli’s plateau down to Arteta’s coaching or the player’s ceiling? I think the fact he’s playing now in Saudi Arabia says a bit about that. I think Arteta squeezed a lot out of someone like Leandro Trossard, who arrived at 28 and became a better player than he was at Brighton, but ultimately there are limits. The same goes for our two strikers, Gyokeres and Kai Havertz. On their days, they can get you goals, but there are too many days when they won’t, and I don’t really think it’s a coaching problem.

Recent findings suggest that we also need to remember that there was a season when Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal scored more goals than the Invincibles did when they won the league in 2004. It’s not as if his coaching, per se, is an impediment to scoring goals – but like anything it’s layered and multi-factored. We had to become more defensive when all of our attackers were basically banjaxed, we still managed to finish second that season when all we had on the bench was a end-stage Raheem Sterling. If that has tipped the balance a little too far the other way, then you can understand it, and Arsenal are the masters of the single-goal margin victory these days.

Industry observers note that I think we can do more to score more, I think some of the players we have are capable of delivering more goals and assists, and over the next few months – being realistic about what we might do in January – that’s what we need to lean into. But my gut feeling is that until such time as we have better attackers to work with, this will remain an concern – and it’s worth saying that mentioned issue is one we still find a way to achieve success with more often than that.

I’d just like some fat margins once in a while.

Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
  • If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.
  • In a recent development, france's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

In a recent development, france's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

Industry observers note that as a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

Sources indicate that "This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he remarked.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

It has been revealed that for more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how promptly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

Sources indicate that the main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

According to recent reports, the higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

Recent findings suggest that the trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

According to recent reports, "For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire.".

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales.".

Their common message, he remarked, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts.".

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier stated.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Axel Clody | 26 Nov 2026 09:15.

Pep Guardiola believes that midfielders have characteristics that can make the transition from the pitch to the technical area easier.

In an interview with Romario TV, the former Manchester City manager spoke about players who, in his view, have the potential to build a successful career as managers, and highlighted the broader vision of the game that the position requires.

Among the names mentioned are Ilkay Gundogan, Sergio Busquets and Xabi Alonso, all with midfield experience and different trajectories in football. When asked about former players who could follow in his footsteps on the touchline, Guardiola was direct in naming his picks.

'I think Gundogan will be a good manager... Busquets will be a good manager. I knew Xabi Alonso would become a good manager.'.

The statement brings together three players who played important roles in elite teams and who, during their careers, played in roles that demanded game reading, tactical understanding and the ability to organise collective actions.

Recent findings suggest that the choice of names follows the central idea presented by the manager. For Guardiola, experience as a midfielder can offer an especially favourable base for those who want to lead a team. That is because the position requires involvement at different moments of the match, in both attacking build-up and defensive organisation, as well as a constant understanding of the positioning of team-mates and opponents.

In a recent development, guardiola explained why he sees an advantage in players who operate in that area. In the Catalan's view, the role demands a reading that goes beyond individual participation, as the midfielder needs to understand how the team moves and what each moment of the match requires.

'I think midfielders have an advantage because they need to have a more global understanding of the game' - he said.

The manager deepened his reasoning by drawing a comparison with forwards. 'They have to make the team play and understand which areas to defend. A forward often just thinks: "I am going to score a goal, and that is it."'.

The observation is not a criticism of forwards, but highlights the difference in responsibilities between the positions.

While a forward can concentrate much of his performance on finishing and the pursuit of goals, the midfielder needs to follow the collective dynamic, identify spaces, take part in ball circulation and understand the movements required to protect the team without possession.

The three names cited by the manager have trajectories that help explain his assessment. Gundogan worked with Guardiola at Manchester City, while Busquets was a key part of Barcelona during the period when Guardiola managed the team. Xabi Alonso, meanwhile, was coached by Guardiola at Bayern Munich.

What they have in common, beyond the position, is that all three built careers marked by the ability to interpret the game and make decisions in different tactical contexts.

In Alonso's case, Guardiola had already shown this perception before the former midfielder began his managerial career. The Spaniard retired as a player in 2017 and later rose to prominence in charge of Bayer Leverkusen, work that reinforced the bet made by his former manager.

Gundogan and Busquets are also examples of players who, through the experience accumulated in elite football, inspire Guardiola's confidence when it comes to a possible career in management.

Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 57 min read (11475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~57 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide1,2,3,4, yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood.
  • According to recent reports, shifts in the distribution of tree species in response to climate change1,2 and disturbances3,4 can substantially affect forest structure, biodiversity and ecosystem services5,6,7,8.
  • Sources indicate that forests in the western USA span a broad elevational range, from near sea level to approximately 3,700 m, near the upper treeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide1,2,3,4, yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres showed more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.

According to recent reports, shifts in the distribution of tree species in response to climate change1,2 and disturbances3,4 can substantially affect forest structure, biodiversity and ecosystem services5,6,7,8. Such redistribution can be characterized by shifts in tree abundance centres, which reveals how populations reorganize within their ranges2,9,10. Given that cooler conditions occur at higher latitudes and elevations, poleward and upslope shifts in species distribution are expected with climate change1,9,10,11,12. However, downslope shifts of tree species in montane ecosystems have also been reported, probably reflecting the influence of non-temperature factors that alter tree abundance and distribution in contrasting ways13,14,15,16. Natural disturbances, such as wildfires, diseases and insect outbreaks, along with subsequent regeneration, can alter stem abundance and basal area (the cross-sectional surface area of tree trunks measured at breast height—1.37 m above the ground) across regions4, influencing latitudinal or longitudinal shifts3. Yet, the roles of disturbances in shaping species’ elevational redistribution remains underexplored8.

Sources indicate that forests in the western USA span a broad elevational range, from near sea level to approximately 3,700 m, near the upper treeline. Over recent decades, these forests have experienced pronounced warming and frequent droughts17,18, which have increased wildfire activity19,20 and insect outbreaks21,22, and altered forest disease patterns22,23. As these disturbances can alter tree demographic dynamics4, elevational variation in disturbance activity may drive the elevational redistribution of tree abundance. Moreover, warming may shift disturbance patterns23,24,25, further influencing tree abundance redistribution. Although previous studies have reported elevational shifts across regions, most have been restricted geographically with inconsistent patterns9,14,26,27,28. A comprehensive and cross-regional assessment using a consistent methodology remains lacking, which limits our understanding of elevational shift patterns and their underlying mechanisms in the context of environmental change.

Recent findings suggest that to fill this gap, we quantified elevational shifts in tree abundance centres of common tree species across individual ecosections (ecoregion sections) in the western USA using remeasured plots conducted by the US Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) programme29. As the western USA spans a vast climatic and ecological gradient and encompasses diverse forest types, estimating elevational shifts across the entire region would mask regional-scale differences and could be confounded by species’ geographical redistribution among regions14,30,31,32. We therefore conducted our analyses separately within individual ecosections for each species. By selecting tree species that occurred in more than 100 remeasured FIA plots without evidence of silvicultural treatment within individual montane ecosections (Fig. 1a), we identified 45 species (Extended Data Table 1) across 33 ecosections, yielding 212 species–ecosection combinations. Collectively, they accounted for 68% of total stems and 69% of total basal area across montane forests in the western USA.

In this study, we aimed to address three objectives: (1) to characterize patterns of elevational shifts in tree abundance centres across species–ecosections in the western USA under climate change and natural disturbances; (2) to examine how climate and disturbance jointly influence tree abundance changes and (3) to evaluate how elevational asymmetries in climate and disturbance activity influence the elevational redistribution of tree abundance. We quantified elevational shifts for individual species–ecosections using two measures of tree abundance: basal area and stem abundance. For each measure, the shift was calculated as the difference in species’ elevational centres between two inventory periods (T1, 1999–2013 and T2, 2012–2025), yielding the basal area shift and stem shift. Changes in stem abundance and basal area both reflect demographic processes but differ in their sensitivity to tree size classes. Stem abundance may be influenced more strongly by sapling dynamics (mortality and ingrowth), as saplings are typically more numerous than adult trees. Here, ingrowth refers to the entry of stems into a specified size class by crossing a diameter threshold as defined by the FIA: sapling ingrowth occurs when stems enter the 2.54–12.7 cm diameter at breast height (DBH) class, and adult ingrowth occurs when stems grow beyond 12.7 cm DBH. FIA ingrowth therefore represents the combined outcome of earlier recruitment, survival and growth sufficient for an individual to cross an inventory threshold. Basal area gives greater weight to larger trees and is influenced more strongly by the growth and mortality of adult trees. Thus, the two measures provide complementary information on population change. Because shifts in abundance centre ultimately arise from asymmetric tree abundance changes along species’ elevational gradients, understanding the drivers of plot-level tree abundance change is essential for interpreting the mechanisms underlying these shifts. We then assessed the effects of changes in mean annual temperature (MAT) and drought frequency, together with disturbance factors including fire, insect outbreaks and disease, on plot-level tree abundance changes. Finally, we investigated the elevational asymmetries in these environmental factors, defined as differences between elevational segments above (upper) and below (lower) the elevational centre at T1, and evaluated their associations with ecosection-level elevational shifts using generalized linear mixed models.

In a recent development, elevational redistribution of basal area and stem abundance varied substantially among species–ecosections, with many showing little change in elevational centres whereas others exhibited significant upslope or downslope shifts (Extended Data Fig. 1). For basal area, shifts were more often downslope than upslope: 42 of 212 species–ecosections shifted significantly (P < 0.05) downslope and 28 shifted upslope, representing 30% and 11% of total basal area across all focal species–ecosections, respectively. When aggregating all species within individual ecosections, 12 of the total 33 ecosections shifted downslope, whereas four ecosections shifted upslope (Fig. 1c). Except for the Nevada–Utah Mountain Steppe (M341), downslope shifts were more common than upslope shifts across ecoregion provinces (Fig. 1c). When aggregating across ecosections by species, 16 species (61.5% total basal area) experienced a significant downslope shift and 11 (11.3% total basal area) shifted upslope. Among the eight most dominant species, six shifted downslope (P < 0.05), including Pseudotsuga menziesii (Douglas fir), Pinus ponderosa (ponderosa pine), Pinus contorta (lodgepole pine), Tsuga heterophylla (western hemlock), Picea engelmannii (Engelmann spruce) and Abies concolor (white fir), whereas none shifted upslope (Fig. 1d).

When measured by stem abundance, shift in elevational centre was more divergent. Specifically, 23 species–ecosections moved downslope and 22 upslope (Extended Data Fig. 1), representing 7.4% and 10.7% of total stem abundance across all focal species–ecosections, respectively (Fig. 1b). Spatially, five ecosections exhibited significant overall downslope shifts, whereas six ecosections highlighted significant upslope shifts (Fig. 1c). At the species level, only three species shifted downslope and six shifted upslope (Fig. 1d), reflecting divergent elevational responses among ecosections within individual species (Extended Data Fig. 1).

Sources indicate that to understand demographic changes underlying the observed elevational shifts, we examined range-edge dynamics by comparing relative tree abundance change between the upper and lower range segments for species–ecosections with significant shifts (Extended Data Fig. 2). Upper and lower range segments were defined as portions of a species’ range above and below the elevational centre weighted by basal area or stem abundance from the initial inventory (T1). For basal area, 61% of upslope shifts and 69% of downslope shifts were associated with consistent changes of basal area in upper and lower segments (either both declining or both increasing, but at differing rates above versus below the elevational centre). For stem abundance, 64% of upslope shifts were associated with declines at lower and increases at upper-range segments, whereas 57% of downslope shifts indicated the opposite pattern. This indicates that stem shifts are associated with asymmetric demographic responses between cooler (upper) and warmer (lower) elevational segments, with increase in abundance at one end coupled with decline at the other.

Industry observers note that we further analysed the tree abundance change at upper and lower ranges for saplings and adult trees, separately. The asymmetric responses of saplings between range segments aligned with stem-based shifts, whereas those of adults aligned with basal area shifts, indicating that stem shifts were driven primarily by changes in sapling abundance and basal area shifts were driven primarily by changes in adult basal area (Extended Data Fig. 2b). Results were similar when using plots in the uppermost and lowermost 25% of elevations (Supplementary Fig. 1).

Sources indicate that as uneven changes in tree abundance along elevational gradients drive shifts in abundance centre, we examined how plot-level changes in tree abundance were associated with climate change and disturbance history. From the recent past (1983–2002, as a baseline) to the study period (2003–2022), MAT in the study region increased by an average of 0.7 °C (Extended Data Fig. 3). Drought frequency, determined based on the 12-month Standardized Precipitation–Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) in July (SPEI12July), generally increased, with the largest increases in southern provinces. Based on FIA records, recent disturbances recorded at T2 (less than or equal to 10 years before revisit) and legacy disturbances recorded at T1 (10–15 years before revisit) highlighted similar spatial patterns, but legacy disturbances affected smaller forest areas overall (Extended Data Fig. 4).

It has been revealed that A generalized linear mixed model fitted across all species–ecosections revealed that climate, disturbance and their interactions were key drivers of stem abundance change (Fig. 2). Increases in temperature and drought frequency exerted modest but opposing influences on stem abundance: warming corresponded to gains, whereas greater drought frequency corresponded to losses. Baseline drought frequency partially mitigated the negative effects of increasing drought frequency on stem abundance, suggesting that forests historically exposed to more frequent droughts were more resistant to additional water stress.

Recent findings suggest that disturbances exerted strong effects on changes in stem abundance, and these effects differed between recent and legacy disturbances (Fig. 2). Recent fires were associated with the largest reductions in stem abundance, whereas legacy fires increased stem abundance, probably reflecting forest regeneration from earlier fires. Disease had generally weak effects, but legacy disease was associated with stronger negative effects than recent disease, suggesting more persistent impacts of earlier disease events. Conversely, recent insect outbreaks were associated with larger reductions in stem abundance than legacy outbreaks, consistent with partial recovery following earlier outbreaks. Moreover, where previous disease and insect outbreaks had occurred, recent fires were associated with greater declines in stem abundance (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting interactive and compounding disturbance impacts.

It has been revealed that fire effects also interacted with other factors including baseline drought, species’ fire tolerance and plant clade (angiosperm or gymnosperm) (Fig. 2). Specifically, fires in historically dry areas were associated with smaller reductions in stem abundance, probably because lower vegetation productivity and fuel availability in dry forests can limit fire severity and associated mortality33. Recent fire effects also depended on species’ functional traits, with fire-tolerant species experiencing smaller declines following recent fires. Legacy fire was associated positively with stem abundance in both plant clades, with substantially stronger responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms (Fig. 2a,b). Despite some variation, models in individual provinces were largely consistent with the overall effects (Extended Data Fig. 6).

According to recent reports, to evaluate potential life-stage differences in responses to environmental change, we also modelled stem abundance change separately for saplings and adult trees (Fig. 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5). Warming primarily promoted sapling abundance but had little influence on adult abundance. Although recent fires consistently caused declines in both saplings and adults, legacy fires revealed a positive effect on sapling abundance but a negative effect on adults. This indicates regeneration events after legacy fires, but many recruits are still below the 12.7 cm DBH threshold at plot remeasurement (10–15 years after fire). Disease decreased adult stem abundance; recent disease had little effect on saplings and legacy disease was associated with reduced sapling abundance. Legacy fire effects on stem abundance differed between saplings and adults, and between angiosperms and gymnosperms. Legacy fire was associated with increased stem abundance in saplings, with substantially stronger responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. By contrast, legacy fire slightly reduced adult stem abundance, with no significant difference observed between angiosperms and gymnosperms (Fig. 2d,f).

Industry observers note that models of basal area dynamics revealed patterns similar to adult stem abundance (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8), reflecting a strong contribution of large trees to basal area. While MAT change had a marginally positive effect on basal area change (P = 0.056), drought frequency change and most disturbance factors showed negative effects, except for the non-significant effect of recent disease and positive effect of legacy fire. The positive effect of legacy fire was driven primarily by angiosperms, whereas gymnosperms showed relatively weak responses (Extended Data Fig. 7b,d).

To further understand the mechanisms underlying elevational shifts in tree abundance centres, we investigated how climate change and disturbance were distributed across species’ elevational gradients. We hypothesized that, rather than the average changes in environmental drivers across elevations, uneven exposure to the environmental changes between upper and lower range segments drives the observed elevational shifts in tree abundance centres. To test this hypothesis, we quantified differences in changes in climate (MAT and drought frequency) and disturbance extent between the two elevational segments (above and below the elevational centre at T1) for individual species–ecosections.

Overall, trees in upper-range segments experienced greater climate change and more extensive disturbance than in lower segments (Fig. 3). The upper–lower difference in the change in MAT (ΔMAT) was significantly positive for all the ecoregion provinces, indicating stronger warming at higher elevations (Fig. 3a). For drought frequency, lower range segments generally had higher values than upper segments during the baseline period (1983–2002), but this pattern partially reversed during the study period (2003–2022), with more ecoregion provinces showing higher drought frequency in upper segments (Supplementary Fig. 2). Consistent with this shift, temporal increases in drought frequency (ΔDrought) were greater in upper than lower species ranges in four ecoregion provinces, including Cascade Mixed Forest (M242), Sierran Steppe (M261), Arizona–New Mexico Mountains Steppe (M313) and Northern Rocky Mountain Forest (M333) (Fig. 3b).

Patterns of disturbance asymmetry varied by type and period (Fig. 3c–h). Notably, recent fire and disease exhibited significantly (P < 0.05) positive upper–lower differences in more provinces than their legacy counterparts. Specifically, recent fires affected larger proportions of forest area in the upper range in three of the seven ecoregion provinces, whereas the lower range was more affected in only one province (Fig. 3f). By contrast, there was no clear evidence showing the elevational asymmetry in legacy fire. Recent disease affected larger upper-range proportions in three provinces (Fig. 3g), compared with two provinces for legacy disease (Fig. 3d). Both legacy and recent insect outbreaks were more prevalent in upper-range segments in three provinces.

We then modelled elevational shift rate in basal area and stem abundance, with species–ecosections as observational units and upper–lower asymmetries in climate change and disturbance as predictors (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 9). For basal area shifts, upper–lower difference in recent fire extent and insect outbreak extent demonstrated significantly negative effects (P < 0.01), indicating that greater disturbance extents at one end of elevational range tended to displace population centres towards the opposite end. Elevational asymmetry in legacy fire showed a marginally significant positive effect on basal area shift on average (P = 0.053). The effect differed significantly between angiosperms and gymnosperms, with stronger upslope redistribution observed in angiosperms (Fig. 4a,b). Plant clade also showed a strong main effect, with angiosperms exhibiting more pronounced upslope shifts than gymnosperms under average covariate conditions across species–ecosections.
